processing: Details are scarce. It is treated here as a green tea, in which the leaf is heated to stop oxidation, then shaped and dried; officials have called for protecting the traditional craft.
harvest_season: Not well recorded; Zhejiang green teas are typically picked in spring.
appearance_dry: Not well recorded; expect the green leaf typical of Zhejiang greens.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear yellow-green, as with other Zhejiang greens.
appearance_wet: Not well recorded; expect soft green leaf, as is usual for the class.
taste_profile: No detailed tasting record exists; as with other Zhejiang greens, expect a fresh, lightly vegetal cup with some sweetness.

brewing.notes: General advice for a Zhejiang green: water off the boil and short steeps.

vintage_note: Specific sales practice is not recorded. As is usual for Zhejiang greens, expect the current spring harvest, best drunk within the year. Dongyang Dongbai is used as a regional brand name.
description:
Dongbai Cha comes from Dongyang, in the Jinhua area of Zhejiang. It is one of the historic names of the region's tea, and Dongyang Dongbai is now promoted as a regional brand.

How it is made today is not well described. Protecting the traditional craft has been called for, while what can be said about the leaf is general to Zhejiang greens: heat, shape, dry.

There is no solid tasting record to pass on. Brew it like other Zhejiang greens, with water around 85°C and short steeps, and see what it gives you.

A visiting tea-association official has described the brand as not yet strong. If you find it, ask for the harvest date and treat the historic name as background, not as proof of quality.
history:
The name goes back to the Tang dynasty: Li Zhao's Guoshi Bu lists Dongbai from Wuzhou, the old name for the Jinhua area, among the notable teas of its time.

Today it is part of Jinhua's tea industry, where it is regarded as a historic tea with room to grow. How closely the modern tea resembles the Tang one is not known.
